title: 7 Physician Scheduling Options for Residencies, Compared
description: Physician scheduling tools for residencies, compared: a managed service, spreadsheets, QGenda, TigerConnect, EZCall, Lightning Bolt and Amion.
content:
Summary

  • GME scheduling is a rules problem, not a simple rota, complicated by strict ACGME rules and the annual loss of expertise when chief residents graduate.
  • Scheduling solutions are divided into two types: self-service software (DIY) which you must learn and operate, and managed services (done-for-you) which deliver a finished schedule.
  • For many programs the harder problem is not finding software but keeping the scheduling knowledge from one chief to the next, which stays with the program whatever tool it uses.
  • Managed services like Scheduling Wizard take the administrative burden off the program, build the rules in while the schedule is made, and keep your program's rules written down, saving dozens of hours a year.

If you've ever watched a chief resident spend their entire winter break hunched over a spreadsheet, cross-referencing rotation requirements, vacation requests, call fairness, and conference leave, then you already know that GME scheduling is not just another doctor's rota.

It's a rules problem. As one healthcare administrator put it in a Reddit thread, "Scheduling is such an important piece. Current software is outdated, AI is just moving so fast, everyone is scrambling."

The challenges that make residency program scheduling categorically different from standard physician scheduling are well-documented. ACGME duty hour rules, including the 80-hour limit averaged over four weeks, in place since 2003, and the 24+4 limit that has applied at every PGY level since 2017, are non-negotiable rules with serious accreditation consequences if violated. On top of that, you have interlocking block rotations, subspecialty training requirements, call fairness mandates, and clinic coordination, all of which must be held in balance simultaneously.

And then there is the July handover: every year, the chief resident who finally cracked the code on your program's scheduling logic graduates. The institutional knowledge walks out the door, and their successor starts from scratch. The cycle of late nights, missed requirements, and resentful residents begins again.

There are more physician scheduling tools than there used to be, but not all of them are built for the complexity of GME. Some take real setup, some are lighter on detailed rules, and some, like Amion, are mostly used to publish a schedule rather than build it.

This guide covers 7 options: a managed service that does the work for you, the spreadsheet, and self-service software and platforms that you operate yourself. For each, we evaluate on the four criteria that matter most to chief residents and program directors: ACGME compliance handling, setup burden, subspecialty rule support, and institutional knowledge transfer.

A note before the list: we are Scheduling Wizard. We build physician schedules as a service, so we have included ourselves below and you should read our entry with that in mind. The order here is by one thing only, who actually builds the schedule, which is why a service comes first and the spreadsheet second; the software and the platforms you publish through follow. Rank by cost, or by how good the mobile app is, and the order changes. We have described the other tools as their own users and documentation describe them.

The Done-for-You Model: Managed Scheduling Services

This model is for programs that want to hand the scheduling burden off entirely, no new software to learn, no knowledge lost to graduation.

1. Scheduling Wizard

Model: Managed Scheduling Service (Done-for-You)

Scheduling Wizard is a managed scheduling service built for medical residency and fellowship programs. Backed by Y Combinator (W26), it was founded specifically to solve the GME scheduling problem, not adapted from a general workforce management tool.

The model is simple: programs submit their rules (residents, rotations, call rules, vacation requests, subspecialty requirements), and our team builds the block, call, clinic and attending schedules. The output arrives as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you, ready for whatever platform your program already uses.

There is no software for your team to learn and no rule configuration for you to get wrong.

Criteria What to expect
ACGME Compliance Handling Built in, to the requirements you give us
Setup Burden Minimal, no software to learn
Subspecialty Rule Support Custom rules per specialty, written down with you
Institutional Knowledge Transfer The written rule set lives with the service, not the chief

A study published in Neurosurgery found that a rebuilt call schedule reduced call variation by 70% and increased residents' perception of fairness from 43% to 95%. That study was not our work, but it shows how much the way a schedule is built matters.

Best for: Chief residents and program directors who want their scheduling weeks back, their schedules inside the ACGME rules, and an end to the cycle of knowledge loss every July.

What you get: finished block, call, clinic and attending schedules in the format your program wants, as Excel or Google Sheets, with a custom live view if you want one. Major redrafts through the year are included. For the specifics, see our page on physician scheduling, done for you. We build to your rules and requests, however granular, with the ACGME requirements among them.

2. Excel / Google Sheets

Model: Manual

Ranked second because it is the honest answer to what residency programs use. Scheduling tools get compared against each other, but the thing a program is usually switching away from is a spreadsheet a previous chief built. It deserves credit for the reasons it persists: free, universal, and able to represent any rule at all.

It also explains why programs start looking. The work does not shrink; it just moves to whoever holds the file. Fairness gets tracked by counting, conflicts get found by reading, and all of it has to be redone when something changes in February.

When programs move from a spreadsheet to scheduling software, the sticking point is rarely generating a draft. It is everything after: confirming the draft holds, fixing what does not, and absorbing the effects of each fix. If that pass is still yours, the license has moved the work rather than removed it.

The DIY Model: Self-Service Scheduling Software

This model is for programs with dedicated administrative staff and the time to invest in learning, configuring, and maintaining a scheduling platform in-house.

3. QGenda

Model: Self-Service Software

QGenda is an enterprise scheduling platform, built for health systems with dedicated scheduling staff. It provides a powerful centralized platform with real-time updates, mobile access, and solid reporting, features that are useful once the system is up and running.

The problem for GME programs is getting it up and running in the first place. QGenda is built for organizations with dedicated IT and administrative resources to configure and maintain it. For a chief resident who has never touched the software and has six months before the new academic year begins, there is a lot to learn.

Criteria What to expect
ACGME Compliance Handling Rules configured by your team
Setup Burden Implementation and training on your side
Subspecialty Rule Support Customizable; your team sets it up
Institutional Knowledge Transfer Depends on who maintains the setup

Best for: Large GME offices or health systems with full-time, dedicated scheduling administrators, not rotating chief residents.

4. TigerConnect Physician Scheduling

Model: Self-Service Software

TigerConnect started as a clinical communication platform and expanded into scheduling, which gives it a natural advantage for programs already embedded in the TigerConnect ecosystem. The scheduling module can automate parts of the annual block schedule creation and integrates with existing workflows to reduce back-and-forth.

It is still a piece of software that must be learned, configured, and maintained, and the configuration knowledge sits with whoever maintains it.

Criteria What to expect
ACGME Compliance Handling Rule-based; configured by your team
Setup Burden Training on your side
Subspecialty Rule Support Admin-configurable rules for departmental needs
Institutional Knowledge Transfer Depends on who maintains the setup

Best for: Programs already using TigerConnect for clinical communication who want an integrated, self-managed scheduling solution.

5. UKG EZCall

Model: Self-Service Software

Now part of the UKG suite, EZCall focuses on the daily management of on-call assignments. Its mobile app lets residents view schedules, request swaps and flag availability.

Its focus is managing the call schedule day to day. Building the master block schedule from a blank page is work the program still does, usually the chief resident.

Criteria What to expect
ACGME Compliance Handling Focused on call; the block schedule is built elsewhere
Setup Burden Setup on your side; master schedule built elsewhere
Subspecialty Rule Support Configurable by your team
Institutional Knowledge Transfer Depends on how the block schedule is built

Best for: Programs whose primary pain point is the daily chaos of on-call swaps and last-minute coverage, not the initial creation of the master schedule.

6. Lightning Bolt (by PerfectServe)

Model: Self-Service Software

Now part of PerfectServe, it generates shift schedules from a rule set you define, which puts it a level above manual builders. It is aimed at programs with complex call patterns that want to run the tool themselves.

As with any rules-based tool, the work is in the configuration. Building the rule set that accurately reflects your program's ACGME rules, subspecialty requirements, and fairness preferences is a significant project. Doing it well requires expertise. And as with every other self-service platform, that expertise leaves with the person who built it.

Criteria What to expect
ACGME Compliance Handling Rule configuration can include work hour rules
Setup Burden Configuration on your side
Subspecialty Rule Support Designed for multi-rule environments
Institutional Knowledge Transfer Rule logic is saved; the reasons behind it depend on your own notes

Best for: Tech-savvy programs with a consistent, long-term administrator, not a rotating trainee, who can invest in mastering a complex but powerful platform.

7. Amion

Model: Publishing Platform

Amion is familiar to most people in GME, and it is a simple, reliable way to publish a schedule. Most programs use it to publish a schedule that was built elsewhere. In that workflow the hard work happens before the schedule goes in, often in what some schedulers call the "BIG Spreadsheet".

Publishing does not keep the reasoning. The published schedule is visible to everyone, but the spreadsheet and the judgment behind it live elsewhere, and can be lost when the chief changes.

Many Scheduling Wizard clients keep Amion as their publishing platform and upload the finished schedule into it; others use our live view, or both. It is entirely up to you.

Criteria What to expect
ACGME Compliance Handling Sits with whoever builds the schedule
Setup Burden Low, easy to upload and share an existing schedule
Subspecialty Rule Support N/A, mostly used for publishing
Institutional Knowledge Transfer The schedule is kept; the reasoning behind it lives elsewhere

Best for: Any program that needs an easy way to publish a schedule that has already been built elsewhere.

Decision Framework: DIY or Done-for-You?

The choice between self-service software and a managed service ultimately comes down to one question: where does your scheduling problem actually live?

If your program's pain is in daily schedule visibility (residents not knowing who's on call, difficulty requesting swaps) a publishing platform like Amion or a communication-integrated tool like TigerConnect may be sufficient.

But if your pain is in creating the schedule (the annual grind, the ACGME compliance anxiety, the awkward knowledge handoff every July), better software alone may not solve it.

Ask yourself:

  • Does our chief resident lose dozens of hours a year to scheduling? That's time that should be spent on clinical training and education.
  • Have we made the same ACGME-adjacent mistake more than once because a new chief didn't know the rules? That is the kind of thing that only shows up later.
  • Are we re-training a new person on complex scheduling software every single year? That's a structural inefficiency, not a training problem.

If you answered yes to any of the above, a managed service is worth a serious look. Services like Scheduling Wizard exist because GME scheduling requires expertise more than a new piece of software. The solution is to have people who do this full time do the work, so your program can focus on what actually matters: training great physicians.

The July handoff problem is real, and it is avoidable. The programs that get past it ask a different question: should we be doing this ourselves at all?

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best software for residency scheduling?

The best solution depends on your program's specific needs and resources. For most GME programs where scheduling is handled by a rotating chief resident, a managed service like Scheduling Wizard is often a good fit, because there is no software to learn and the build is off the chief's plate. For large hospital systems with dedicated, full-time schedulers, self-service software like QGenda can be a good option.

How does a managed service handle the ACGME rules?

By putting the rules into the schedule while it is built. Instead of a user entering rules and chasing flagged errors, we write the ACGME requirements you tell us apply, the 80-hour average, call frequency, days off, the subspecialty rules, down with you and build to them from the start. There is still a review at the end; it is a check, not a repair job.

Can I still use Amion if I use a managed scheduling service?

Yes. It is entirely up to you. They deliver the finished schedule as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you, and you put it into whatever viewing platform your program already uses.

Our program has very specific rules. Can a service handle them?

Yes. A key advantage of a managed service is its ability to handle highly specific and unique program rules. Services like Scheduling Wizard write down a custom rule set for each program. This includes complex subspecialty requirements (e.g., for Neurosurgery or Anesthesiology), call fairness definitions, specific rotation sequences, and individual resident requests, so the finished schedule is built to them.

What happens to scheduling knowledge at the July handover?

Each July, critical scheduling knowledge is lost when the experienced chief resident graduates, forcing their successor to start from scratch. This cycle leads to inefficiency, errors, and resident dissatisfaction. One way to solve it is a managed service, which writes down and keeps your program's rules. This keeps continuity, so the rules and the definition of fair carry over from year to year, regardless of who is in the chief resident role.
